chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who has goods with him as deposits, which remain with him for a year, two years, or more than that. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no Zakat upon him until he sells it, unless he was given it as his capital wealth, so he withholds it seeking profit (price increase). So when he does that, Zakat becomes obligatory upon it; but if he was not given it as his capital wealth, there is no Zakat upon him until he sells it; and if he withholds it for whatever reason he withholds it, then when he sells it, upon him is only the Zakat of one year.'
ai.seo_question: When is Zakat due on goods held for trade or speculation?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through the chain of Samaanah, clarifies the Shia juristic distinction between trade goods held as capital (ra's al-mal) versus those held for other purposes, establishing that Zakat is primarily triggered upon the actual sale or conversion to cash rather than mere possession. It highlights the principle that if goods are held for speculation without being treated as primary capital, the Zakat liability is limited to the year of sale, reflecting a nuanced approach to commercial assets in Shia fiqh. This ruling underscores the importance of intent and the nature of the asset in determining the timing and scope of Zakat obligations.
